business_model.claim: Euroseas operates as one operating and one reportable segment—operating container carriers—evaluated by consolidated net income, with no geographical breakdown because charterers trade vessels worldwide.
quotes: As a result, the Company’s management, including the CODM, reviews operating results solely by consolidated net income of the fleet, and thus the Company has determined that it operates under one operating and one reportable segment, that of operating container carriers.
When the Company charters a vessel to a charterer, the charterer is free to trade the vessel worldwide and, as a result, the disclosure of geographical information is impracticable.

business_model.claim: Charter revenue is driven primarily by fleet size, revenue-earning voyage days, and daily charter rates, with fleet utilization of 99.7% and an Average TCE rate of $29,107 per day per vessel across an average of 22.22 vessels in 2025.
quotes: Our charter revenues are driven primarily by the number of vessels in our fleet, the number of voyage days during which our vessels generate revenues and the amount of daily charter revenue that our vessels earn under charters, which, in turn, are affected by a number of factors, including our decisions relating to vessel acquisitions and disposals, the amount of time that we spend positioning our vessels, the amount of time that our vessels spend in drydock undergoing repairs, maintenance and upgrade work, the age, condition and specifications of our vessels, levels of supply and demand in the transportation market, the number of vessels on time charters, voyage charters and in pools and other factors affecting charter rates in the containership market.
Utilization Rate (percent) | 99.7% | 99.7%
While employed, our vessels generated a TCE rate of $29,107 per day per vessel in 2025 compared to a TCE rate of $28,054 per day per vessel in 2024, an increase of 3.8%.
In 2025, we operated an average of 22.22 vessels, a 2.3% increase over the average of 21.73 vessels we operated during the same period in 2024.

business_model.claim: Fixed-term time charters insulate contracted revenue from market swings until renewal, whereas index-linked charters and expiring contracts follow market rates; as of August 2026, charter coverage was over 95% for the remainder of 2026, 81% for 2027, and 47% for 2028.
quotes: The average TCE rate our vessels achieve is a combination of the time charter rate earned by our vessels under time charter contracts, which is not influenced by market developments during the duration of the fixed term time charter (unless the two charter parties renegotiate the terms of the charter or the charterer is unable to make the contracted payments or we enter into new charter party agreements), and the TCE rate earned by our vessels employed under time charters linked to an index and voyage charters, which is influenced by market developments.

Our charter coverage is over 95% for the remainder of 2026, 81% for 2027 and 47% for 2028, ensuring that our profitability will remain strong regardless of the levels at which expiring charters are renewed.

business_model.claim: Market charter rates depend on global containerized trade demand, tariffs, geopolitical route disruptions such as Red Sea rerouting and Strait of Hormuz risks, and fleet supply—where the global containership fleet stood at approximately 33.29 million teu with approximately 12.18 million teu on order as of April 15, 2026.
quotes: Container shipping markets experienced substantial gains in 2024 and 2025, driven by rerouting away from the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and Suez Canal due to Houthi attacks on ships.

If further tariffs are imposed on a broader range of imports, or if retaliatory trade measures are enacted by affected countries, these factors could reduce demand for containership trade, result in the loss of customers, and harm our competitive position in key markets.

Specifically, as reported by industry sources, the capacity of the fully cellular worldwide container vessel fleet, as of April 15, 2026, was approximately 33.29 million teu with approximately another 12.18 million teu, or about 36.58% of the fleet capacity on order.

We paid a total of $6.57 million in charter commissions for the year ended December 31, 2025, representing 2.8% of Voyage revenue, compared to commissions of $6.49 million for the year ended December 31, 2024, representing 3.0% of Voyage revenue.

The segments in which we operate—feeder and intermediate containerships—not only have a significantly smaller orderbook as a percentage of the existing fleet but also have an older age profile.
This is likely to result in very modest fleet growth, or potentially even fleet shrinkage, in these segments.

competitive_position.claim: The worldwide cellular containership fleet had an orderbook of approximately 12.18 million teu, or about 36.58% of existing fleet capacity of approximately 33.29 million teu, creating oversupply risk.

An over-supply of containership capacity may result in a reduction of charter rates.

competitive_position.claim: Charter rate gains in 2024 and 2025 were supported by rerouting away from the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, and Suez Canal, and the reversal of those inefficiencies threatens future charter rates.
quotes: Container shipping markets experienced substantial gains in 2024 and 2025, driven by rerouting away from the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and Suez Canal due to Houthi attacks on ships.
These disruptions have resulted in inefficiencies and support for container rates, which may not continue once these are resolved.
The eventual reversal of these inefficiencies, together with the absorption of the increased fleet orderbook, presents challenges for our sector over the medium term.

competitive_position.claim: U.S. and retaliatory tariffs, trade policy uncertainty, and slower economic growth in China, the Asia Pacific region, Europe, or the United States threaten containerized trade demand and Euroseas's competitive position.
quotes: If further tariffs are imposed on a broader range of imports, or if retaliatory trade measures are enacted by affected countries, these factors could reduce demand for containership trade, result in the loss of customers, and harm our competitive position in key markets.

Because a significant number of the port calls made by our vessels involves the loading or discharging of containerships in ports in the Asia Pacific region, economic turmoil in that region may exacerbate the effect of any economic slowdown on us.

competitive_position.claim: Euroseas depends on a limited number of liner customers in a consolidating industry, exposing the company to charter counterparty default or renegotiation risk.
quotes: Our dependence on a limited number of customers operating in a consolidating industry;

Liner companies, which comprise the largest contingent of charterers of containerships, have been placed under significant financial pressure, thereby increasing our charter counterparty risk which may have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations.

competitive_position.claim: Declines in vessel market values can trigger financial and collateral covenant breaches under secured credit facilities, force capital raises or asset losses, and constrain dividend capacity.
quotes: A decrease in the market values of our vessels could limit the amount of funds that we can borrow or trigger certain financial covenants under our current or future credit facilities, and we may incur a loss if we sell vessels following a decline in their market value.
If the assessed market value of our vessels declines below certain thresholds, we may violate these covenants and may be required to restore the breach of our credit agreements.

competitive_position.claim: Euroseas's reliance on affiliated manager Eurobulk and affiliations with principal officers create potential conflicts of interest that could be detrimental to the company.

Uncertainties related to the price of fuel, and our reliance on suppliers;

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in the 2025 Form 20-F Item 3.D risk factors.
growth_thesis.claim: For containership demand and charter rates to remain supportive, major economies must sustain containerized trade growth without severe tariff disruptions.
quotes: We anticipate that the future demand for our container vessels and the charter rates of the corresponding markets will be dependent upon economic recovery and growth in the United States, Europe, Japan, China and India and the overall world economy as well as seasonal and regional changes in demand and changes to the capacity of the world fleet.

If further tariffs are imposed on a broader range of imports, or if retaliatory trade measures are enacted by affected countries, these factors could reduce demand for containership trade, result in the loss of customers, and harm our competitive position in key markets.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in the 2025 Form 20-F Item 3.D and August 2026 Form 6-K CEO commentary.
growth_thesis.claim: To avoid charter rate erosion despite a global orderbook equal to 36.58% of existing fleet capacity, net fleet growth in Euroseas's feeder and intermediate segments must remain limited.
quotes: Specifically, as reported by industry sources, the capacity of the fully cellular worldwide container vessel fleet, as of April 15, 2026, was approximately 33.29 million teu with approximately another 12.18 million teu, or about 36.58% of the fleet capacity on order.
The segments in which we operate—feeder and intermediate containerships—not only have a significantly smaller orderbook as a percentage of the existing fleet but also have an older age profile.
This is likely to result in very modest fleet growth, or potentially even fleet shrinkage, in these segments.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in the 2025 Form 20-F Item 3.D and August 2026 Form 6-K.
growth_thesis.claim: Sustaining elevated re-chartering rates upon contract expirations depends on whether Red Sea and Middle East routing inefficiencies persist or are offset by underlying demand.
quotes: Container shipping markets experienced substantial gains in 2024 and 2025, driven by rerouting away from the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and Suez Canal due to Houthi attacks on ships.
However, any meaningful easing of geopolitical disruptions could reduce freight rates and tonne-mile demand, potentially placing downward pressure on charter rates.
The eventual reversal of these inefficiencies, together with the absorption of the increased fleet orderbook, presents challenges for our sector over the medium term.

quotes: If, at the time of sale, the carrying value is less than the sales price, we will realize a gain on sale, which will increase our earnings, but if, at the time of sale, the carrying value of a vessel is more than the sales price, we will realize a loss on sale, which will negatively impact our earnings.

A decrease in the market values of our vessels could limit the amount of funds that we can borrow or trigger certain financial covenants under our current or future credit facilities, and we may incur a loss if we sell vessels following a decline in their market value.
